title: Pneumonic plague, by the numbers | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The World Health Organization said Wednesday that it had few clear answers about the recent death of a worker at a Russian institute that researched plague. The death, the subsequent isolation of hundreds of co-workers and close contacts, and reports that another worker may have pneumonia have fueled global concern about a rare form of plague.

Here’s what we know about pneumonic plague by the numbers.

One personwho worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in southeast Russiahas died.

There have also been media reports that asecond employeeof the lab has pneumonia of “undetermined cause,” the director-general of the World Health Organization said Wednesday.

The28-year-oldwho died was identified by the independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala as Darya Shipilova.

Shipilovafirst wentto the hospitalSeptember 29in Shelekhov, a town12 milessouthwest of Irkutsk, where she worked.

Three days later, onOctober 2, she died.

Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease, says the worker died of pneumonia of “unknown” origin and downplayed suspicions that her death was related to her work.

WHO said it has seen local media reports about an incident in the lab involving a broken test tube. Currently, “I know what you know from the media of the test tube breaking and exposure,” Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of WHO’s department of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said Wednesday.

OnOctober 2, the Russian government held a meeting “because they suspected a resident of the Irkutsk Institute had contracted a dangerous infection,” WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday.

WHO said it first heard about the patient because it uses AI to monitor local news reports for illnesses of concern.

Under international law, Russia should have reported the incidentwithin 24 hours.

After the WHO sought more information about the death, the Russian Federation replied Tuesday to say that “no caseof plague had recently been reported.”

The Russian government also said it placedabout 200 peoplewho’d had contact with the worker in quarantine or under close follow-up,WHO said.

WHO said it had requested further information from the government, but has not received it.

“We don’t have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” Tedros said. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”

A number of hospitals in the area have restricted visitors and are conducting comprehensive health checks, including requiring people to fill out questionnaires about “plague” and other infectious disease symptoms. Rospotrebnadzor, however, reassured people in the region where the lab operates that the “epidemiological situation” is stable.

About 95 peoplework at the Anti-Plague Institute.

The instituteopened in 1934to research plague. The bacterium that causes plague, Yersinia pestis, still circulates among wildlife in Siberia and neighboring regions.

Globally, more than200kinds ofmammals, mostly rodents, can contract Y. pestis,studies show. Marmots are the most common carriers in Siberia.

WHO’s early assessment, based on reports that the cause of death was pneumonic plague, was that the risk to the general public appeared to be low.

There are thousands of suspected plague cases around the world every year, Van Kerkhove said.

From 2019 to 2025,10 countriesreportedalmost 4,000suspected human plague cases and423 deaths, WHO said Wednesday.

Central Asia has the largest number of foci, or areas where the disease is present. People are most often infected after exposure to infected rodents.

There arefour major types of plaguecaused by Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body:

WHO said it conducted an initial assessment of risk based on an understanding that the Russian lab worker’s case could be pneumonic plague.

Pneumonic plague isthe only formof the bacterial infection that can spread from person to person.

The basic reproduction number isabout 1.1 to 1.3, meaning thatone personwith pneumonic plague can spread the disease through a cough or sneeze to about1.3 people,studies show. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.

People can develop symptomsas soon as 24 hoursafter exposure, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center. Typically, people with pneumonic plague are so sick that they rarely spread it because “it’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” he said.

There’s also very limited travel to the US from this area. There areno direct flightsbetween Russia and the US, Dalal noted. A spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services saidabout 200 travelersfrom the region arrive in the United States over the course of a year.

“These travelers arrive at designated airports where CDC personnel are already positioned and prepared to identify potential health concerns, conduct public health assessments, and take appropriate action when warranted,” the HHS spokesperson said.

By the time infected travelers reached the US, they would already be showing symptoms, Dalal said.

“Of course, you have to be careful,” he said, because “the world is a little village now,” as everyone learned during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Patients treated withinthe first 24 hoursof infection have the best chance of surviving.

People with plague typically get at least10 to 14 daysof antibiotics.

Five antibioticstypically work best against plague: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin and streptomycin.

Doctors have used plague vaccines since the19th century, but it’s not clear how protective they are against pneumonic plague.WHO doesn’t recommendvaccination except for high-risk groups and lab workers who are regularly exposed to the bacteria.

The bacterium that causes plague circulates onevery continentexcept Oceania.

It has infected human populations forat least 5,000 years, studies of archaeological sites show.

Three of the world’s deadliest pandemicswere caused by Y. pestis.

1924was the year ofthe last documentedperson-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the US, during an outbreak in Los Angeles.

Sincethe 1990s,most human cases have been in Africa,according to WHO.

July 2025was when the last person in the US died from pneumonic plague. The person lived in Arizona and was probably infected while working with sick cats. In the USaboutfivehumancases are reported every year.
